claims.text: On-the-fly active-learning MLIPs can replace full AIMD in thermodynamic-integration workflows.
The proposed workflow can yield fusion free energies and high-temperature thermodynamic properties with less than 5% error.
The proposed workflow will cost approximately one order of magnitude less than direct AIMD workflows.
Brief AIMD runs at selected temperatures can provide configurations sufficient to train a Gaussian-approximation or neural-network interatomic potential on the fly.
The trained MLIP can be used for long molecular-dynamics thermodynamic-integration calculations of free-energy differences.
The proposed workflow applies to solid fcc Al, solid fcc Ni, solid B2 NiAl, and their corresponding liquids near melting.
The intended test domain is ambient pressure, 0.8–1.2 times the melting temperature, and compositions of pure Al, pure Ni, and equiatomic NiAl.
The trained MLIP acts as a surrogate for the ab initio potential-energy surface.
Reproducing ab initio energies and forces across sampled configurations allows the MLIP to capture anharmonic vibrations.
Reproducing ab initio energies and forces across sampled configurations allows the MLIP to capture electron–phonon coupling.
Low-cost, extensive MLIP molecular-dynamics sampling enables evaluation of vibrational entropy and free-energy integration.
For the elemental and binary test systems, MLIP thermodynamic integration will reproduce AIMD fusion free energies within 5%, characterized as approximately 0.02 eV per atom.
The MLIP workflow will be approximately 10 times faster than direct AIMD workflows.
For NiAl, the MLIP workflow will be approximately 5 times faster than TOR-TILD.
The method is valid for metallic systems containing no more than two components under ambient pressure from 0.8 to 1.2 times their melting temperature.
Extrapolation of the MLIP may produce uncertainty of ±10–20% in free-energy differences.
Transferability to compositions more complex than binary alloys has not been tested.

contradictions.description: The predicted fidelity permits fusion-free-energy errors up to 5% or approximately 0.02 eV/atom, whereas the latent-heat falsification threshold is 0.1 kJ/mol, approximately 0.001 eV/atom. Thus, a result could satisfy the stated primary error prediction yet still be declared falsifying under the much stricter derived-observable criterion.
